time.desc: The incoming national leader filed an application with the Supreme Court to suspend the legal "strip or take down" cutoff for short video platforms to allow the new government to gain room for negotiations.

The federal government filed papers in the Supreme Court asking that the incoming national leader's request for a moratorium be dismissed, while the platforms asked to block the law's implementation on free speech grounds.

The Supreme Court held an oral argument on the short video platform ban case. During the hearing, most judges paid more attention to national security reasons and were skeptical of the platform’s claims.
The Supreme Court rejected the platform’s request for emergency relief and maintained the “strip or take it off” legal arrangement to take effect as scheduled.
The platform briefly stopped services in the country and was removed from major app stores, causing user-side access interruptions.

The platform resumed services to domestic users because the incoming national leader publicly promised to suspend law enforcement through administrative means and provide service providers with liability guarantees.

The current government has publicly stated that it will not enforce the relevant ban on the statutory effective date, and will hand over subsequent enforcement responsibilities to the incoming new government.
The new government signed an executive order to postpone the implementation of the ban on short video platforms by about two months to buy time to reach a deal plan.

Major app stores resumed the listing of the short video app in the country, and the regulatory authorities provided a written guarantee that they would not pursue relevant distribution responsibilities during the extension window.
State leaders signed a new executive order, once again extending the "divest or take it off" cutoff by about two months to move forward with deal negotiations.

After the country announced to impose additional tariffs on the other country, the other country made it clear that it would not approve the platform transaction, causing the nearly completed sale plan to be shelved.

The judicial department emphasized that the control of platforms by foreign parent companies poses a serious threat to national security and called them powerful espionage tools. On the same day, the platform first defended freedom of speech.
During the oral argument, most judges expressed doubts about the platform’s claims and tended to support legislation based on national security considerations.
Lawyers for the leader-elect submitted a brief to the court stating their clear "opposition to banning the platform" and requesting a delay in taking effect to seek a political solution.
Leaders publicly stated that they are negotiating with multiple parties to acquire the platform and said they would make a decision on the sale within dozens of days.

Leaders signed an executive order instructing relevant agencies to establish a sovereign wealth fund within a year, saying it may be used to acquire the platform
